name: Dread perming

lead: Dread perming is a way to get a dreadlocks hairstyle by combining backcombing with a chemical perm. It is often used on straight hair to give it texture and speed up locking, producing a locs look in a single long appointment.

The appearance payoff is the finished style: defined, uniform locs without the many months of natural locking. The method is described in encyclopedic and salon sources; no clinical research has tested it.

paras: Hair of roughly six inches or more is divided into sections, each section is backcombed, then set by perming it as is, twisting it or wrapping it on curlers. The chemicals make strands swell and lose their shape, and as they shrink back the hair keeps the form it is held in. Sessions can take over six hours, with maintenance visits about every six months and tightening sprays in between, per Wikipedia.

Chemical processing can damage hair and irritate the scalp, and allergic reactions are possible, according to consumer-oriented sources. Salon cost is cited at roughly $300 to $400, with maintenance around $200 or more. Anyone with a history of reactions to hair chemicals is usually advised to patch test.

chain: Chemical perm swells and sets each section
angle.text: The perm gives straight or loosely textured hair a locs appearance in one long session instead of many months of natural locking.

lead: Dread perming is a chemical method of creating or maintaining dreadlocks, used by salons and at home. The hair is treated so strands become frizzy and bind together, and further treatment sets them into locs.[1]
It is often applied to straight hair to add texture and shorten the locking period. Over weeks to months the hair loosens and can come to resemble naturally formed locs.[1]

Dreadlocks themselves have a long history across African, South Asian, Rastafari and other traditions, and are also made naturally, with crochet hooks or by backcombing.[2] Dread perming is one modern shortcut among these.
No clinical studies have examined the procedure; information comes from encyclopedic and salon sources.

paras: Wikipedia describes the process as sectioning the hair, backcombing each section into a dread shape, and then perming it flat, twisted or wrapped around a curler. The chemical causes each strand to swell and lose its original shape, which it then retains as it contracts.[1]

Locs can form naturally in very curly hair, be started with crochet hooks or backcombing, or be added with faux and soft locs. Dread perming is a chemical option, typically relevant for straighter hair.[2]
Consumer and salon articles list chemical damage to hair, scalp irritation and allergic reaction as downsides, and note that full locking can still take well over a year.[1]
